name: Potassium
short: Case reports: fatal or near-fatal high blood potassium from salt substitutes or supplements; a report says it is commonest with kidney impairment, ACE inhibitors, ARBs or potassium-sparing diuretics.
text: Case reports describe severe high blood potassium (hyperkalaemia) from potassium taken by mouth as salt substitutes or supplements: two patients had near-fatal hyperkalaemia with cardiac arrest, one after salt-substitute intake and one from a muscle-building supplement, and both were resuscitated and survived; two patients with an impaired ability to handle and excrete extra potassium, due to chronic heart failure, azotaemia and spironolactone, developed severe hyperkalaemia and serious cardiac arrhythmia after excessive use of potassium-containing salt substitutes; an 88-year-old man with chronic kidney disease developed marked hyperkalaemia (7.5 mEq/L) without symptoms after unknowingly eating a potassium-enriched salt substitute in hospital; and a case-report letter is titled "Fatal hyperkalemia from a salt substitute" (no abstract is available). One of these case reports states that severe hyperkalaemia from oral potassium is extremely rare if kidney function is normal and occurs most commonly in people with kidney impairment or those taking potassium-sparing diuretics, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) or ACE inhibitors, and it lists muscle weakness, ascending paralysis and gastrointestinal effects, including mucosal necrosis that may lead to perforation, among the features of potassium toxicity. In a report on five patients already taking potassium-sparing diuretics or potassium supplements, serum potassium rose when the ACE inhibitor captopril was added and three developed laboratory-diagnosed hyperkalaemia; the authors called the combination a potentially important drug interaction. In the run-in phase of a clinical trial in 191 people with chronic kidney disease stage G3b-4 (83% taking renin-angiotensin system inhibitors), two weeks of potassium chloride raised plasma potassium by 0.4 mmol/L on average and 21 participants (11%) developed hyperkalaemia; they were older and had higher baseline potassium. In contrast, in relatively healthy people a meta-analysis of 20 short-term trials (1216 participants) found that a moderate oral potassium supplement caused only a small rise in blood potassium (0.14 mmol/L) and no change in kidney function, and in a trial in 20,995 people with a history of stroke, or aged 60 or over with high blood pressure, serious adverse events attributed to hyperkalaemia were not significantly more frequent with a potassium-enriched salt substitute than with regular salt (3.35 vs 3.30 per 1000 person-years). A Cochrane review of 26 salt-substitute trials found they probably increase blood potassium slightly in adults (6 trials, 784 participants) and may make little to no difference to hyperkalaemia (5 trials, 22,849 participants), but all the trials excluded people in whom extra potassium is known to be potentially harmful and no trials in pregnant women were found, and the reviewers said this lack of evidence limits conclusions on safety in the general population.
